newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission statement on Annual Economic Report.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission statement on Annual Economic Report.

text.p: The following is the text of a statement by the European Commission that accompanied the release on Thursday of its 1997 Annual Economic Report:
1997 Annual Economic Report - Growth, employment and convergence on the road to EMU

The European Commission has adopted its 1997 Annual Economic Report. The report presents the Commission's views on the economic situation and the main economic policy issues facing the European Union (EU) and the Member States. The report analyses the growth and job performance of the EU economy as a whole over the first half of the 1990s as well as the more favorable outlooks for 1997-1998. It identifies several important macroeconomic obstacles to growth and job creation within the EU economies. It also presents the employment and unemployment experience of a number of Member States which have achieved a significant reduction in unemployment in recent years. The report analyses the impact of globalisation and rapid technological advances on the Union economies. It also highlights the need for continued efforts to improve the responsiveness of Europe's labour markets. Finally, the report explains the need for determined efforts to consolidate and reshape the public finances of Member States. The report

The Annual Economic Report is presented at the initiative of Yves-Thibault de Silguy, Commissionner responsible for Monetary and Economic Affairs. Its aim is to initiate a debate on the economic policy options to be considered in the forthcoming 1997 Broad Economic Policy Guidelines. The Commission invites comments on the report from all interested parties, including in particular the European Parliament, the Economic and Social Committee, the social partners, and the Committee of Regions.
Disappointing growth and job performance in the first half of the 1990s

Over the period 1991-96, economic growth in the Union economy was 1.5 per cent per year on average. Total employment declined by 4 1/2 million jobs. On this account, the performance of the EU over the first half of the 1990s was much worse than that of the United States and worse also than that of Japan.

The disappointing output and job performance was mainly the result of macroeconomic obstacles to growth within the Community. In the late 1980s/early 1990s, inflationary pressures arose due to the insufficient expansion of productive capacity, overly lax budgetary policies and inappropriate wage increases. This led to high real interest rates, undermined exchange rate stability and resulted in the 1992/93 recession. High real interest rates and currency turmoil were responsible also for the faltering of the recovery between mid-1995 and mid-1996.
Progress towards EMU is helping to overcome growth obstacles

EMU will help Member States to overcome the obstacles to sustained growth and job creation. The adoption of the single currency will eliminate exchange rate instability among participating countries. The stability-oriented economic policy framework in EMU, which has been reinforced by the agreement on the Stability and Growth Pact at the Dublin European Council, will result in lower real interest rates, stronger, investment and can be expected to lead to enhanced price and wage discipline. This fundamental change in the overall macroeconomic policy mix will be favourable to growth and job creation.

Substantial progress in preparations for EMU and budgetary adjustments in many Member States have already brought important benefits. Interest rates have converged towards lower levels and exchange rate stability has improved. Based on sound monetary and budgetary policies, a recovery in economic growth is underway in the Community. Output growth is expected to pick up to around trend rate in 1997 and above its trend in 1998. Union-wide unemployment is expected to decline in 1997 and 1998 but the level will remain high.

Supply-side fundamentals -- in terms of low inflation, prospects for moderate wage increases and strong investment profitability - are healthy and improving further. Together with a credible stability-oriented framework in EMU, this provides the basis for achieving strong and durable economic growth over the medium term.
Globalisation and technological improvements are not the causes of unemployment

The 1997 Annual Economic Report examines the link between employment trends in the Union and the processes of globalisation and rapid technological advances. The report finds that these factors put constant pressures on Member States to maintain or improve their competitive position but that they have not caused the high level on unemployment in the European Union.

Technological and organisational advances and improved international resource allocation have been and will continue to be the key driving forces behind improvements in productivity, economic growth and living standards. However, such developments have implied and will continue to imply continuous changes in the EU structure of output and employment. Furthermore, they tend to reduce the demand for low-skilled labour.

In order to reap the potential benefits of improved technology and globalisation it is essential that economic growth is strong enough to re-employ the resources freed by higher productivity. In addition, structural measures need to be taken (i) to improve education and training and the employment opportunies for low-skilled workers, and (ii) to ensure that efficiently functioning goods and services markets facilitate sectoral changes in a smooth and socially acceptable manner.
Need for greater labour cost flexibility and employment

Persistently high unemployment in the Community points to a twofold problem. Firstly, relative to stable labour productivity growth, macroeconomic growth in the Community has been insufficient to create an adequate number of jobs.

Secondly, following the first oil price shock, high wage and non-wage labour costs as well as, in some cases, rigid employment security rules reduced the attractiveness of labour as a production factor. This evolution compelled enterprises to keep up a substitution of labour by capital in order to safeguard their competitiveness. However, labour markets in the Community have adjusted gradually, leading to a considerable improvement in profitability. This has laid the ground for economic growth sustained by capacity-widening and employment- creating investment as demand prospects brighten. But this development impacts only slowly on the employment-intensity of growth.

Another, more rapid route towards a more employment- intensive pattern of growth would be to encourage a significant downward widening of the labour cost scale as in the United States. This would enable activities with low productivity to remain and/or to become profitable. But for social and political reasons, an emulation of the US-approach which has led to a significant drop in real wage income for low-skilied labour is neither feasible nor desirable in the Community. Hence, the need for strong, investment-supported macroeconomic growth.

Nevertheless, there is a continued need to improve the responsiveness of Member States' labour markets to changes in the economy through a modernisation of the organisation of work, increased geographical and professional mobility. In addition, pragmatic approaches to achieve a widening of the labour cost structure, such as a lowering of non-wage costs or reduced income taxation for the low-skilled and temporary entry-wages for disadvantaged workers, should be pursued. Action in these fields would increase the employment-intensfty of growth.

In sum, in order to transform the current recovery into strong and durable growth supported by higher investment, to significantly reduce unemployment and to preserve, in a reformed and streamlined fashion, the key ingredients of the European social model, it is essential that Member States adopt measures in line with the conclusions adopted by the European Councils in Florence and Dublin.
